interest: This file offers a compelling juxtaposition of outside public commentary and internal State Department planning regarding Japanese industrial concentration before and during World War II. The 1940 correspondence from C. P. Monningh provides a unique perspective on how American corporatist thinkers interpreted Japan's state-directed monopoly policy in Manchoukuo and occupied China—not merely as military imperialism, but as an orderly bulwark against Communism that could inspire domestic economic reform by replacing competition with planned private monopolies ('Industrial Monocracy'). In contrast, the 1944 memorandum by Frank P. Lockhart documents high-level U.S. wartime deliberations on the postwar deconcentration of the Zaibatsu, highlighting the tension between immediate military occupation controls and long-range economic reconstruction aimed at integrating Japan into a liberal, multilateral world trade order.
overview: This file (decimal 894.602) covers U.S. Department of State records between February 1940 and November 1944 relating to Japanese monopolies, cartels, and corporate industrial organization in East Asia. It begins with a February 1940 proposal from Los Angeles attorney C. P. Monningh to Secretary of State Cordell Hull enclosing a synopsis on 'Industrial Monocracy,' which evaluates Japan's monopolistic enterprises in Manchoukuo and occupied China as anti-communist measures and advocates an American system of private national monopolies, followed by a formal acknowledgment from Maxwell M. Hamilton of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs. The file concludes with a November 1944 memorandum from Frank P. Lockhart to Charles F. Remer assessing a policy prospectus by Rudolph on the Japanese cartel system, analyzing the applicability of President Roosevelt's anti-cartel directives for Germany to Japan, addressing the role of the Zaibatsu, and debating whether short-term military occupation directives might conflict with long-term economic rehabilitation and non-discriminatory multilateral trade.

subfiles.about: Letter from C. P. Monningh to Secretary of State Cordell Hull presenting his interpretation of Japanese monopolies in Manchoukuo and China as a strategy against Communism.
subfiles.summary: C. P. Monningh, an attorney in Los Angeles, writes to Secretary of State Cordell Hull offering an interpretation of Japanese economic activities in East Asia. Citing an article by John E. Orchard in the January 1940 issue of Asia magazine on Manchoukuo's corporate monopolies and Five-Year Plan, Monningh argues that Japan's establishment of state-sanctioned monopolies is an attempt to counter Communism. He notes that Japan is planning provincial monopolies in conquered China and that War Minister Shunroku Hata recently defended a rice monopoly in Japan. Monningh requests information on Asian monopolies from the State Department and encloses a synopsis of his own economic reform ideas.
subfiles.title: Letter from C. P. Monningh to Secretary of State Cordell Hull on Japanese Monopolies

subfiles.about: An enclosed theoretical synopsis outlining 'Industrial Monocracy', an economic system aimed at eliminating commercial competition through planned national monopolies.
subfiles.summary: This enclosure details Monningh's proposed economic system of 'Industrial Monocracy' (or 'Industrial Monocarcy'), which advocates for the worldwide elimination of business competition. Under this plan, private merchants would surrender patents and assets in exchange for shares in privately owned national corporations operating as monopolies for each industry. Monningh asserts that this reorganization would eradicate poverty, panics, and crime, simplify government by repealing all anti-trust laws, and limit business regulation strictly to surplus profit caps. He suggests the program could be established through the repeal of anti-trust statutes, industrial balancing, and martial law.
subfiles.title: Synopsis of 'Industrial Monocarcy' by C. P. Monningh

subfiles.about: Formal acknowledgment from the Department of State to C. P. Monningh regarding his letter and enclosed article on 'Industrial Monosracy'.
subfiles.summary: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Chief of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, writes on behalf of Secretary of State Cordell Hull to acknowledge receipt of C. P. Monningh's letter of February 2, 1940 (cited as February 3). Hamilton states that the letter and its enclosure, an article entitled 'Industrial Monosracy', have been noted with care. He expresses appreciation for Monningh's civic spirit in bringing his economic concepts to the attention of the Department.
subfiles.title: Letter from Maxwell M. Hamilton to C. P. Monningh Acknowledging Letter on 'Industrial Monosracy'

subfiles.about: Internal State Department memorandum by Frank P. Lockhart evaluating Rudolph's prospectus on the post-war Japanese cartel system and long-range economic policy.
subfiles.summary: Frank P. Lockhart submits observations to Charles F. Remer on a draft prospectus by Rudolph concerning the Japanese cartel system. Lockhart agrees that President Franklin D. Roosevelt's letter setting policy on German cartels is applicable to Japan and notes that Rudolph's analysis implicitly addresses the Zaibatsu system. However, Lockhart cautions that short-term measures enacted by military occupation authorities could conflict with long-term remedial economic policies, reiterating his objections to committee document CAC-222. Citing concerns raised by Herbert Woolley during a conference in Emilio G. Collado's office, Lockhart questions whether Rudolph's proposals for eliminating economic aggression and integrating Japan into unrestricted multilateral trade can be reconciled with broader departmental economic policy.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from Frank P. Lockhart to Charles F. Remer on Japanese Cartel System Prospectus
